plan_fact_checks.claim: Plan section 3.1 and section 16 item 5: the Wazuh official small-deployment baseline is 4 vCPU, 8 GiB RAM, 50 GB for 1-25 agents; the 100 GiB disk of the lab VM is a planning reserve, not a verified requirement.
plan_fact_checks.evidence: documentation.wazuh.com/current/quickstart.html in search results: sizing table 4 vCPU / 8 GiB / 50 GB for 1-25 agents (storage for 90 days of alerts), 8 vCPU / 8 GiB / 100 GB for 26-50 agents, 8 vCPU / 8 GiB / 200 GB for 51-100. The 100 GiB lab disk therefore exceeds the 1-25 agent baseline; the 4 vCPU and 8 GiB match. Caveats from the same results: the server page asks for 20 GB free on the /var/ossec volume before the first start, the quickstart metadata looked old, and the installation guide references Wazuh 4.14.

plan_fact_checks.claim: Plan section 4, section 5 week 7 and section 16 item 4: Sysmon network connection Event ID 3 is not enabled by default; it must be verified and selectively configured.
plan_fact_checks.evidence: learn.microsoft.com/en-us/windows/security/operating-system-security/sysmon/sysmon-events ('Sysmon events') in search results: Event ID 3 is disabled by default because of volume and should be enabled selectively. 'Enable and configure Sysmon in Windows' (how-to-enable-sysmon) says Sysmon itself produces nothing until installed and configured. A Microsoft Q&A answer states that installing without a configuration file does not capture network events (community answer, not official text).

plan_fact_checks.claim: Plan section 4, section 13 and section 16 item 1: HTB published path estimates are 342 hours for the Penetration Tester path and 189 hours for the SOC Analyst (CDSA) path (about 531 hours together), and are not course quotas; the SOC Analyst path must be completed before the CDSA exam.
plan_fact_checks.evidence: help.hackthebox.com/en/articles/12741910-academy-modules-paths ('Academy Modules & Paths') in search results: Penetration Tester (CPTS) 42 days 6 hours = 342 hours; SOC Analyst (CDSA) 23 days 5 hours = 189 hours; HTB computes a day as an 8-hour study session; estimates are averages. The 'not course quotas' framing is the plan's own and is consistent with the article saying they are averages. The SOC Analyst path page (academy.hackthebox.com/path/preview/soc-analyst) lists 15 modules, and the CDSA certification page (academy.hackthebox.com/preview/certifications/htb-certified-defensive-security-analyst) says all modules of the path must be completed first (search summary). 342 + 189 = 531 hours, matching the plan's arithmetic.

Some cached pages still label v19.2 as current. The v20.0 detailed change list was not in the results.

plan_fact_checks.claim: Plan section 5 week 7: Windows Kerberos Event 4769 or RC4 type 0x17 alone is not proof of Kerberoasting.
plan_fact_checks.evidence: INFERRED, not confirmed by any source: no result states the claim. learn.microsoft.com 4769 reference and 'Detect and Remediate RC4 Usage in Kerberos' in search results: 0x17 is RC4-HMAC; Microsoft's guidance is to filter 4769 for 0x17 to find accounts and services that still depend on RC4, with causes such as accounts lacking AES keys and non-Windows clients. The Microsoft pages do not mention Kerberoasting, so the conclusion is INFERRED from the documented benign causes.

plan_fact_checks.claim: Plan section 5 week 7 authoring expansion: Windows Security IDs 4624, 4625, 4688, 4720 and 4698 and Sysmon IDs 1, 3, 11, 22 depend on audit and Sysmon collection settings.
plan_fact_checks.evidence: Partly confirmed only: the Windows Security IDs and Sysmon IDs 1 and 3 rest on Microsoft pages, but Sysmon IDs 11 and 22 appear in no Microsoft result (TryHackMe room text only), so the claim as worded is NOT_CONFIRMED. Microsoft Learn results: 4624 (logon, needs logon auditing), 4625 (failure), 4688 (needs Audit Process Creation under Detailed Tracking; the command line field needs a separate 'Include command line in process creation events' setting and is empty by default), 4698 (Audit Other Object Access Events subcategory), 4720 (Audit User Account Management). Sysmon ID 1 and 3 appear in the Microsoft 'Sysmon events' result text; IDs 11 (file create), 13 (registry value set) and 22 (DNS query) were seen only in TryHackMe room text returned by search (Windows Logging for SOC, Detecting Persistent DLL Attacks, RDP lateral movement analysis), not in a Microsoft result.
